01

The Shelf Is Checkable

Josiah: “imagine like smoke shops — are you trying to figure out if they got specific papers or what flavor wood they might have at the time.”

No tiny, cluttered corner-shop energy: glass cases, a merch wall, room to breathe.

Josiah: “I'm thinking like a whole store bro — I'm willing to go all in.”

Clean and Clean-Cut

The shop they visited to buy the K is the standard: spotless, organized, merch on the wall. If it looks sloppy, it's wrong.

No Cigar Room

Fair Prices, Always

The incumbents overcharge; Smoke Cartel wins by being fair and still eating. Never become the overcharger.

Owners Who Smoke

The vision

The store we're aiming for.

Josiah's direction for the store itself, whichever area wins.

  • A whole, clean store. Not a tiny, cluttered corner shop. Glass cases, room to breathe, a merch wall — we'd rather take our time and open right than force a bad space.
  • No cigar room. Cut on purpose — that's an older generation's habit, not where the money is going. Floor space goes to papers, woods, glass, vapes, and merch.
  • A vending machine inside. It pulls attention and moves the small stuff — papers, lighters, wraps — without tying up the counter.
  • Near food, in a mini-mall. Foot traffic that already exists beats traffic you have to manufacture. A dead strip in the wrong neighborhood kills a good store.
  • Owners on the floor. A Black-owned, young-owned shop run by Lucian and Josiah themselves — people who know the products, can read a customer, and price fair instead of overcharging.
  • Young owners, real tech. The online shelf check, social media run like it matters, and AI doing back-office work older shops won't pay for. That gap is the edge.

Maryland · in order

The legal steps.

The order matters: licenses need the LLC, the loan needs the licenses and a location, and the zoning letter comes before any signature on a lease.

  1. Lock the name and the conceptDone

    Smoke Cartel — clean store, online shelf check, no cigar room. (55.TRXKS was the working name; it stays on as the partners' handle.) The brand and the pitch are set. Maryland name check: SDAT entity search — no match found, Nov 5, 2026.

  2. Run the market searchDone

    Six candidate areas scored on college demand, rent, and both partners' drives — see the Locations tab. Recommendation made; decision still open.

  3. Form the LLC in MarylandYou are here

    File Articles of Organization with SDAT (Maryland Business Express), with a Maryland resident agent. This is the step that makes Smoke Cartel a real legal thing — and the wall that keeps the store's debts off Lucian and Josiah personally.

    $100 by mail · $150 online (expedited)

  4. Sign the operating agreementNot started

    Maryland doesn't require one — do it anyway. It puts the 50/50 split, who runs what, how pay works, and what happens if one partner wants out, in writing while everything is friendly.

    $0 with a template · one lawyer review is worth it

  5. Get the EINNot started

    The LLC's federal tax ID from the IRS. Free, online, about 15 minutes. Needed for the bank account, taxes, and hiring — and it's one of the documents SPS asks for to open the wholesale account. Never pay a site for this; the IRS gives it away.

    $0 · irs.gov

  6. Open the business bank account + set up the booksNot started

    Business account in the LLC's name, both partners on it, bookkeeping from the first dollar. Business money and personal money never mix — that's what keeps the LLC's protection real.

  7. File the $300/year Form 1 — every April 15Yearly

    Maryland's Annual Report + Personal Property Return with SDAT. Owed every year whether the store made money or not; missing it can cost the LLC its good standing.

    $300/year · due April 15

  8. Register for Maryland taxesNot started

    Sales & use tax and tobacco tax accounts with the Comptroller, plus the ESD (vape) tax setup — Maryland charges 20% on vapes and larger liquid, 60% on liquid containers 5 mL or less, collected at the register.

    $0 to register

  9. Get the county retail licensesNot started

    Issued by the Clerk of the Circuit Court in the county where the store sits: cigarette retailer, Other Tobacco Products (OTP) retailer — rolling papers, pipes, and hookahs live here — and Electronic Smoking Devices retailer, with a separate ESD license now required under SB 249 (Ch. 415, 2026). Yes, licenses are required — this is the step Josiah flagged to confirm.

    Cigarette retailer $300 (Bus. Reg. §16-302) · OTP retailer $15 (§16.5-203), waived to $0 for cigarette retailer license holders · ESD retailer $300 (§16.7-202) — $600 total for this shop, per the Maryland Code

  10. Get the zoning verification letter — before signing anythingNot started

    Written confirmation from the county that tobacco retail is allowed at the exact address. Non-negotiable and first: Baltimore County passed Bill 68-26 on smoke-shop zoning in 2026, and Baltimore City proposed pausing new tobacco licensure authorizations Oct 2026–Oct 2027. No letter, no lease.

  11. Lock the real estateNot started

    Zoning letter → letter of intent (LOI) → lease with licensing and financing contingencies, or an SBA-backed purchase → permits → buildout. Josiah's rule applies either way: no tiny, cluttered corner box.

  12. Permits, insurance, and the counter rulesNot started

    Buildout, occupancy, and signage permits for the space; business insurance bound before opening; and the Maryland layout rules baked into the build: cigarettes, OTP, and vapes displayed behind the counter in employee-only space, 21+ only, ID anyone who looks under 30 — state law since the Tobacco Retail Modernization Act (2024), not a suggestion.

  13. Open supplier accounts, stock, and openNot started

    Buy only from licensed Maryland wholesalers — that's what the OTP and ESD licenses require. First order is the $125.50 SPS shelf on The Money tab. Then: photograph what actually arrived, flip the shelf search to real counts, soft open, grand opening.

The Working Papers

The documents themselves.

Swipe to flip through them.

LLC Filing Packet — page 1 of 4

Real estate · the process

From zoning letter to keys.

  • 1 · Zoning verification letter. County confirms in writing that a smoke shop can operate at the specific address. This comes before every other real-estate step — a signed lease on a non-conforming address is a trap.
  • 2 · Letter of intent (LOI). Non-binding terms — rent or price, term, buildout allowance, contingencies — so both sides know the deal before lawyers bill for it.
  • 3 · Lease with contingencies, or SBA purchase. A lease should be contingent on the retail licenses issuing and financing landing. Buying runs through the SBA process in the finance plan below.
  • 4 · Permits. Buildout, occupancy, and signage permits with the county — filed once the space is secured, before work starts.
  • 5 · Buildout. Glass cases, shelving, the merch wall, the vending machine, POS — with tobacco and vapes behind the counter by law.

Taxes · the short version

How the LLC gets taxed.

Josiah's question: two partners, one LLC — what's the best tax setup?

  • Default: taxed as a partnership. A two-member LLC is automatically taxed as a partnership — no election needed. The LLC pays no income tax itself; it files Form 1065, each partner gets a K-1 for their 50%, and the profit lands on their personal returns. Pass-through, no double tax.
  • The catch: each partner owes 15.3% self-employment tax on their full share of profit. Early on, build-out losses also pass through to the partners — which helps in year one.
  • Later option: S-corp election. Once the store is solidly profitable, the LLC can file Form 2553 to be taxed as an S-corporation: owners take a reasonable salary (payroll taxes apply) and profit above salary comes out without self-employment tax on that part.
  • The call: start as a partnership, elect later. Year one is thin margins and simplicity wins. When the store is printing, run both sets of numbers with a CPA on real profit and file the 2553 if the savings beat the payroll hassle.

Step 1 of 5

Finance · the SBA plan

What it actually takes in cash.

Josiah's question: loans exist — but how much cash do we have to put up to make the store ours?

First, the correction to the “10% down” idea: SBA 504 is 10% down for a standard, established business — but 15% for a startup (under 2 years), and 20% if it's a startup and a special-purpose property. Smoke Cartel is a startup, so budget 15%. Second: 504 covers real estate and equipment only — not inventory. Inventory and working capital are SBA 7(a) territory. Third: the down payment was never the whole bill.

Route A — Buy a ~$200k property (SBA 504)

Cash to open, buyingEstimate
Total project (property ~$200k + buildout/fees ≈ $260k)≈ $260,000
Down payment at 15% (startup rate)≈ $39,000
Plus licenses, insurance deposits, opening costson top
Cash to be ready with≈ $39,000 + opening costs

At the standard 10% the down payment would be ≈ $26,000 on the same project — don't budget on it. And the 504 loan itself won't stock the shelves: the first inventory comes from savings or a 7(a) line.

Route B — Lease a storefront (the faster route)

Cash to open, leasingLean estimate
First month + security depositincluded below
Clean buildout — glass cases, fixtures, POS, vending machineincluded below
Opening inventory, licenses, insurance, signageincluded below
All-in, lean, for ~1,500 SF≈ $48,000 – $78,000

The honest read: leasing gets the doors open sooner and for less total cash, without owning the building; buying builds equity but ties the loan to the property and the bigger down payment. Either way the savings target is real money split two ways — which is why Money is its own lane in the tracker. One more honesty note: SBA loans carry a personal guarantee, so while the LLC is a real wall for ordinary business debts, that wall has a door in it on the loan. Sign knowing that.

The Palace · the theme

55.TRXKS · WEST BALTIMORE

The theme is a walk up the palace steps: a grand Medellín mansion raised into a royal palace — Babar's palace, the elephant king's house, all calm confidence and ceremony — in ivory and gold, with a Colombian hacienda's arches, marble, and courtyard garden underneath, rebuilt by two young Black owners from West Baltimore. Nothing about it borrows from the drug trade: no portraits, no piles of cash, no crime imagery. Just architecture, atmosphere, and ownership. The owners' own mark hangs at the top of every page — deep royal purple and gold — and the king himself keeps his post in the corner.

The theme

Medellín bones, raised to a palace.

Two homes in one palace: a Colombian hacienda's architecture, and the Baltimore the owners actually come from.

The palace sets the architecture. A Medellín mansion's bones — the grand arch, the colonnade, room after room off a central courtyard — raised to royal scale: palace steps at the entrance, twin columns flanking the great arch, a crown crest at the keystone. Each tab is a room; the home page is the courtyard you arrive in. Inside the arches: ivory walls, antique gold that catches light without raising its voice, and deep palace-garden green growing where plants would grow — in the dividers, the eyebrows, the garden drifting past the windows.

The marble is where the two homes shake hands. A Medellín mansion runs on marble floors; a Baltimore rowhouse announces itself with a white marble stoop, scrubbed clean on purpose, generation after generation. Same stone, same gesture: white marble at the threshold, kept with pride. It runs through this site as soft grey-gold veining in the ivory — in the entrance arch, in the panels — the stoop and the palace floor in one material.

And Baltimore brings the brick and the color. Rowhouse brick and formstone in the seal, and the shop's own goods as the palace's one riot of color. They don't hang in a frame: on the Shop tab, cutouts of everything the shop will carry are scattered straight onto the site's own cream as a collage, because here the wall is part of the site. Everywhere else the paint stays ivory, gold, marble, and green: wealth, space, calm royal confidence.

Black-owned is the foundation, not a feature. This palace is being built by Lucian and Josiah — two young Black owners — for their own community, at empire grade, with fair prices as a palace rule. The luxury isn't a costume borrowed from somebody else's story. It's what ownership looks like when it's done properly.

Palace rules

The rules of the palace.

  1. Gold never shouts

    Antique gold is for rules, numerals, plaques, and the light catching an edge — never a flood, never a glare competing with the room. A palace doesn't yell about money; it just has the marble down. If a gold element is the loudest thing on the page, it's wrong.

  2. Cream is the canvas

    Warm cream — sampled straight from the owners' own hand-drawn logo — is the ground everything stands on: every room, every panel, every table. Nothing sits on black. The brightness is the point: serene, grand, and calm, the way a storybook palace feels at midday.

  3. Everything in its place

    The palace staff keeps it so: symmetrical rooms, generous air, thin gold double-rules like palace trim, each thing where it belongs. If a page feels cluttered, it fails the palace test before any other.

  4. One collage wall

    The Shop tab is the palace's single riot of color — a collage of cutouts of everything the shop will carry, scattered straight onto the cream with no frame and no backing between the goods and the palace: hookah and glass, caps and candles, hoodies and snacks. Everywhere else the paint stays ivory, gold, marble, and garden green. One collage wall is majesty; ten would be noise.

  5. Only the owners' own marks

    The marks on these walls are the partners' own: the hand-drawn Smoke Cartel logo, the real crown cropped from it, the elephant king, and the shop's own goods cut out for the collage wall. No stock logos, no borrowed crests, nothing that belongs to somebody else's brand.

In the store · planning stage

How the palace lands in the room.

The plan for the physical store, when there is one. None of this exists yet.

  • Arches over the cases. The glass cases sit under arched openings, courtyard-style, so the floor reads as rooms off a colonnade — space and calm, not a cluttered counter in a box.
  • Marble at the threshold. White marble at the entry, Baltimore-stoop style, kept clean on purpose — the first thing under your feet says the palace is cared for.
  • The collage wall. The site's Shop-tab collage — cutouts of everything the shop carries, scattered on the cream — printed large behind the counter as the palace's one unrestrained wall, and the merch wall beside it, under the owners' mark.
  • Green, alive. Real plants in the corners like a palace courtyard garden, and gold kept to the fixtures and the lettering. The rest of the room stays ivory and serene.
